title: The Marginal Call
primary_metric: net cost per board foot of black walnut actually sold within the planning quarter (average unit cost, penalized for the carrying cost of any board footage locked in but not sold this quarter)

options.A: The Steady Order -- lock in the shop's usual (smaller) kiln-drying run size, financed comfortably within the existing credit line
options.B: The Full Kiln -- lock in a larger run size that lowers the raw average cost per board foot, financed only if a same-day bank call clears in time

Page carries no explicit last-updated date, and volume discounts are listed (1,000-2,000bf: 5% off; 2,000-4,000bf: 10% off; over 4,000bf: 15% off) but are not applied here -- this case's own average-cost curve is modeled via the fixed-cost/overtime structure in MA1/MA3, not this mill's discrete discount schedule.

sources.note: 2025 median pay $45,310/year, $21.79/hour. Converted to a per-board-foot labor cost ($2.50/bf) using an assumed 8.7 board-feet-per-labor-hour standard-capacity processing rate (MA2) -- no public per-board-foot labor-hour standard exists for furniture-grade walnut.

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Renata Osei, operations manager of a small furniture workshop

deliverables.text: A total production-cost function C(x), where x is the number of board feet of black walnut locked into today's kiln-drying run: using Appendix A's fixed run cost, per-board-foot variable cost, and overtime-labor cost coefficient, combine them into a single cost function in x.

Using the quotient rule, differentiate the average-cost function A(x) = C(x)/x with respect to x, set A'(x) = 0, and solve algebraically for the board footage x* that minimizes average cost -- showing every step of the quotient-rule algebra. Then use the first derivative test to confirm x* is a minimum and not a maximum.

An average-cost comparison table: evaluate A(x) = C(x)/x at three board footages -- x* from D2, The Steady Order's board footage, and The Full Kiln's board footage (Appendix B) -- showing every calculation, and state which of the two real options has the lower average cost and by how much, in dollars and as a percent.

A net-cost-per-board-foot-sold calculation for both The Steady Order and The Full Kiln: using Appendix C's sellable-board-footage limit and carrying-cost rate, determine how many board feet (if any) of each option would go unsold this quarter, add the resulting carrying cost to that option's total cost from D1, and divide by the board footage actually sold -- not the board footage produced -- to get each option's real net cost per board foot sold.

An original visual display (a graph of A(x), built in Desmos or by hand, or an equivalent chart) showing average cost versus batch size, with x*, The Steady Order's board footage, and The Full Kiln's board footage all labeled.

A one-paragraph financing memo: using Appendix D's deposit percentages and credit-line limit, calculate in dollars how much additional financing The Full Kiln requires beyond the existing credit line, and state what happens to the deposit already committed if the bank call does not clear before the mill's last slot fills.

appendices.title: This Quarter's Sellable Limit and Carrying Cost

balance.argument_a: The Steady Order's raw average cost per board foot (D3: $18.50/bf, at 2,000 bf) is only 1.1% higher than The Full Kiln's raw average cost ($18.30/bf, at 3,000 bf) -- a thin gap on paper. But every one of The Steady Order's 2,000 board feet fits inside Appendix C's 2,700 bf sellable limit, so its net cost per board foot actually sold (D4) equals its raw average cost: $18.50/bf, no carrying-cost penalty at all. A is also the only option financeable entirely within the shop's existing credit-line headroom [Appendix D], with no dependency on a same-day bank call clearing before the mill's last slot fills.
balance.argument_b: The Full Kiln genuinely lowers raw average cost (D3: $18.30/bf vs $18.50/bf) by spreading the run's fixed cost over more board feet -- real, correctly-computed calculus, not a trick. The flaw in stopping there is Appendix C: only 2,700 of The Full Kiln's 3,000 board feet can be sold this quarter, so 300 board feet sit as unsold inventory carrying a real cost. Once D4 folds that carrying cost into the total and divides by board feet actually SOLD (2,700, not 3,000), The Full Kiln's net cost climbs to $20.43/bf -- 9.45% higher than The Steady Order's $18.50/bf. B's quantitative case is real only if a Hero can show Appendix C's sellable limit is higher than stated (case.json.modeling_assumptions[MA6].sensitivity), or is willing to argue the financing risk and volume-discount upside are worth paying a real, computed premium for.
balance.margin_basis: margin = |net_cost_per_bf_sold(Steady Order) - net_cost_per_bf_sold(Full Kiln)| / max(...), where net_cost_per_bf_sold(x) = [C(x) + carry_per_bf * max(0, x - sellable_limit)] / min(x, sellable_limit), C(x) = F + v*x + k*x^2. F=$1,800 (MA1), v=$17.40/bf ([S1]+[S2]+[S3]/MA2), k=0.0001 $/bf^2 (MA3), steady=2,000bf (MA4), full=3,000bf (MA5), sellable_limit=2,700bf (MA6), carry_per_bf = 5% x v = $0.87/bf ([S4], quarterly-converted). NC(Steady)=$18.50/bf (fully sold, no penalty). NC(Full)= ($54,900 + $0.87x300)/2,700 = $20.43/bf. margin = |18.50-20.43|/20.43 = 9.45%, within the case's 8-15% target band and SPEC §2's 20% cap. Full arithmetic verified by sensitivity_model.py.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Fixed cost per kiln-drying run (mill run-booking fee + shop changeover/setup labor)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Neither hardwood-kiln operator found in research (Kitsap Dry Kiln, Timms Sawmill) charges a separate flat run-booking fee -- both price per board foot or a small flat processing charge -- so no public figure exists for this specific line item. $1,800 combines a modest kiln-scheduling fee with roughly a day of shop changeover/setup labor at a blended shop rate.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Sets the scale at which raw average cost is minimized (x* = sqrt(F/k) = 4,242.64 bf). At +/-50% flex this does not flip which of the two REAL options (Steady Order vs. Full Kiln) wins -- see case.json.sensitivity_disclosure.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Board feet of finished stock processed per labor-hour at standard capacity, used to convert [S3]'s $21.79/hr wage into a per-board-foot labor cost
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source publishes a per-board-foot labor-hour standard for furniture-grade black walnut processing; chosen to keep the derived labor cost in a plausible range alongside the sourced lumber and kiln-drying figures.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Sets the flat v term, which shifts both options' cost by the same amount rather than changing the gap between them -- not independently flexed in sensitivity_model.py (bundled into v, which is treated as cited/derived, not a stated assumption).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Overtime-labor cost coefficient, k, in C(x) = F + vx + kx^2
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public source models capacity-constrained marginal cost as a precise function for a small furniture shop. The coefficient is a smooth, continuous approximation of a real, well-documented mechanism -- federal law requires 1.5x pay for hours worked beyond the standard workweek -- applied as a stated scenario simplification.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tier 2 P5 found +/-50% flex on k does not flip which real option wins (see case.json.sensitivity_disclosure) -- it moves x* and the theoretical minimum cost, but The Steady Order and The Full Kiln stay on the same side of that minimum either way.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Protagonist-specific: the shop's standing order size with this mill, built up over years of smaller custom runs.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Tier 2 P5 found a +50% flex (to 3,000 bf) collapses The Steady Order into an exact tie with The Full Kiln's board footage, producing a mechanical TIE rather than an independent economic instability -- see case.json.sensitivity_disclosure for the CAVEAT.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Protagonist-specific: stated as the mill's minimum board footage to qualify for its last, deep-discount kiln run this season -- the run size both Renata and the competing national chain are bidding for.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The single most load-bearing protagonist-specific number in the case: it is compared against Appendix C's 2,700 bf sellable limit (MA6), which is what creates the unsold-inventory penalty at the center of the case's trap. Tier 2 P5 found +/-50% flex on this value alone does not flip the verdict (see case.json.sensitivity_disclosure).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: This quarter's sellable limit (hotel order + standing accounts)
modeling_assumptions.basis: Protagonist-specific: the total finished-furniture board footage the hotel's bulk order and the shop's other standing accounts will realistically consume within the five-week window.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the case's load-bearing, dilemma-flipping dial. Tier 2 P5 found a +50% flex (to 4,050 bf) removes The Full Kiln's unsold-inventory penalty entirely and flips the recommended option from The Steady Order to The Full Kiln, since 3,000 bf then fits entirely within the sellable limit and only the raw average-cost advantage remains.

modeling_assumptions.basis: Matches the Background's own stated deadline verbatim -- not an independent estimate.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: None -- fixed by the narrative, not a sensitivity lever.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Available headroom on the shop's existing line of credit
modeling_assumptions.basis: Protagonist-specific: the shop's credit line carries an unstated total limit but is already partially drawn for ongoing payroll and materials, leaving this much available for a new deposit.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Sets the exact dollar gap D6 asks students to compute for The Full Kiln's financing risk ($27,450 deposit - $25,000 headroom = $2,450 gap); does not change the D3/D4 cost-per-board-foot math or margin_pct.

sensitivity_note: T4 tier requirement (SPEC §3): the case requires stating and defending at least one assumed quantity. Six are stated (MA1, MA3-MA6, MA8); MA6 (this quarter's sellable limit) is the dilemma-flipping one -- see modeling_assumptions[MA6].sensitivity and sensitivity_disclosure below.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: How many board feet the hotel order plus standing accounts will actually absorb within a five-week window is a forecast of future demand for one specific, never-before-attempted order size -- not a measurable present fact. Tier 2 P5 found this dial flips the verdict from The Steady Order to The Full Kiln at +50% flex (4,050 bf vs. the stated 2,700 bf), because it removes The Full Kiln's unsold-inventory penalty entirely. This is the case's single most load-bearing, dilemma-flipping assumption, consistent with modeling_assumptions[MA6].

Renata's own typical order size is an estimate of a future/typical pattern for a shop that has never run at this scale before, not a measurable fixed fact -- there is no external record to look up. Tier 2 P5 found +50% flex (2,000 -> 3,000 bf) makes this value numerically identical to The Full Kiln's stated 3,000 bf, producing an exact TIE rather than a directional flip. This is a real result of the flex arithmetic (two independent assumptions landing on the same value at this specific percentage), disclosed here rather than treated as a hidden fragility; it does not generalize to other flex percentages the way sellable_limit's instability does.
